title: Un, le ou du : choisir l'article et le genre
summary: Choose articles for identified things, general categories and uncounted quantities; combine them with à and de.
objectives: Distinguish definite, indefinite and partitive articles.
Use reliable gender clues without treating them as guarantees.
Form au, aux, du and des and recognise familiar definite-article contexts.

sections.title: Choose the noun's gender, then decide whether it is identified
paragraphs: Indefinite articles introduce a countable item: un (masculine), une (feminine), des (plural). Definite articles identify something known or a whole category: le, la, les. Le and la become l' before a vowel or silent h; plural les does not elide. Un hôtel (m., a hotel) therefore gives l'hôtel. With an aspirated h, a conventional sound boundary blocks elision even though h is not pronounced: le héros (the hero). Learn such nouns with their article.

Endings are clues, not proof. -tion and -sion are usually feminine, as in une invitation and une décision; -ment and -age are often masculine, as in un document and un garage. But une page, une image and une plage (a beach) are feminine, while un million is masculine despite -ion. A final written e alone does not establish gender: un problème is masculine.
points: A new singular countable noun normally needs an article or another determiner.
A noun's grammatical gender remains the same when its article becomes l'.

examples.french: J'ai **une** invitation. **L'**invitation est ici.
examples.english: I have an invitation. The invitation is here.
examples.note: Introduce the item, then refer to the identified item.

examples.french: **Le** problème est simple.
examples.english: The problem is simple.
examples.note: Un problème is masculine despite its final e.

examples.french: **La** page est blanche.
examples.english: The page is white.
examples.note: Une page is an exception to the common masculine -age pattern.

mistakes.why: Hôtel has a silent h and requires elision; it is also masculine.

sections.title: A portion uses a partitive; a general preference uses the definite article
paragraphs: For an unspecified amount, use du before a masculine noun, de la before a feminine noun, de l' before a vowel or silent h, and des for plural quantities. These are called partitive articles when they present an uncounted portion; des also serves as the plural indefinite article with countable items. English often leaves some or any unspoken; French normally keeps the article.

A whole category takes le, la or les, especially after verbs expressing likes: aimer le thé means to like tea generally. Contrast drinking some tea with liking tea as a category. Un thé can instead mean one serving of tea.
points: Du pain is some bread; le pain can mean the identified bread or bread in general.
Vocabulary: le pain (m., bread), la soupe (f., soup), l'eau (f., water), les épinards (m. plural, spinach).

examples.french: Je prends **du** pain et **de la** soupe.
examples.english: I am having some bread and soup.
examples.note: Both amounts are unspecified.

examples.french: Nous avons **de l'**eau et **des** épinards.
examples.english: We have some water and spinach.
examples.note: Elision before eau; plural des with épinards.

examples.french: J'aime **le** thé, mais je prends **un** café.
examples.english: I like tea, but I am having a coffee.
examples.note: The general category contrasts with one serving.

mistakes.why: De la elides to de l' before eau.

sections.title: À and de combine with le and les
paragraphs: When the preposition à meets definite le, write au; à + les gives aux. De + le gives du; de + les gives des. There is no contraction with la or l': à la, à l', de la, de l'. A preposition is a linking word such as to, at or from. Du can therefore be either a quantity article or the combination de + le; read the sentence to decide.
points: À + le = au; à + les = aux; de + le = du; de + les = des.

examples.french: Elle va **au** marché, puis **à la** banque.
examples.english: She goes to the market, then to the bank.
examples.note: Le marché (m., market) contracts; la banque (f., bank) does not.

examples.french: La porte **du** garage est ouverte.
examples.english: The garage door is open.
examples.note: Here du means de + le, not some.

examples.french: Il parle **aux** enfants **des** voisins.
examples.english: He speaks to the neighbours' children.
examples.note: Aux combines à + les; des combines de + les.

mistakes.why: À + le must contract when le is the article.

sections.title: French keeps the definite article in several places English omits it
paragraphs: Use definite articles for languages as nouns and academic subjects: le français, les mathématiques. But after parler a language is commonly bare: parler français. Titles normally take the article when speaking about someone: le professeur Martin, la docteure Roy. Direct address usually omits it: Bonjour, docteure !

For body parts whose owner is clear, French often prefers the definite article, especially with a reflexive verb: elle se lave les mains. Some familiar descriptions also use definite articles for the person's clothing or parts of it: elle a les mains dans les poches. The context makes clear whose hands and pockets are meant. Do not extend this to every clothing sentence: elle enlève son manteau (she takes off her coat) normally uses a possessive. Possessives also remain possible for body parts when ownership or contrast needs emphasis.
points: Vocabulary: une main (f., hand), une poche (f., pocket), un manteau (m., coat), le français (m., French language).

examples.french: **Le** français est utile. Je parle français.
examples.english: French is useful. I speak French.
examples.note: Language as subject has an article; after parler it is omitted here.

examples.french: **La** docteure Roy arrive.
examples.english: Doctor Roy is arriving.
examples.note: Mentioning a professional by title differs from addressing her.

examples.french: Elle se lave **les** mains.
examples.english: She washes her hands.
examples.note: The reflexive construction makes the owner clear.

examples.french: Elle a **les** mains dans **les** poches.
examples.english: She has her hands in her pockets.
examples.note: The subject identifies the owner in this familiar body-and-clothing description.

sections.title: Choose the meaning before choosing the article
paragraphs: Ask what the noun represents here: a whole category, an identified thing, one countable item or an unspecified amount. The same noun can change between these readings. A preference verb does not force every following noun into a category: aimer mon quartier expresses affection for a particular neighbourhood, not neighbourhoods in general.

When English has no article, French may still need one. A general dislike keeps its definite article; denying that any quantity is available normally gives de/d'. These are different messages, not two interchangeable ways of saying the same thing.
points: Vocabulary: un poulet (m., chicken as an animal or whole bird); du poulet (chicken as food); un quartier (m., neighbourhood).

examples.french: La ferme élève **des poulets**. À midi, nous mangeons **du poulet**.
examples.english: The farm raises chickens. At noon, we eat chicken.
examples.note: Countable animals and an unspecified amount of meat use different article readings.

examples.french: J'aime **les quartiers calmes**, et j'aime beaucoup **mon quartier**.
examples.english: I like quiet neighbourhoods, and I really like my neighbourhood.
examples.note: The category takes les; the particular place can have a possessive.

examples.french: Je n'aime pas **le miel**, mais je n'ai pas **de confiture**.
examples.english: I do not like honey, but I do not have any jam.
examples.note: Le miel (m., honey) is a category in the first clause. La confiture (f., jam) is an absent quantity in the second.

examples.french: **La patience** aide pendant un long voyage.
examples.english: Patience helps during a long journey.
examples.note: La patience (f.) names an abstract quality generally; English omits the article.

sections.title: Use an ending as a hypothesis, then verify the noun
paragraphs: Several endings help with unfamiliar words: -isme is normally masculine, while many nouns in -té or -tié are feminine. But a familiar exception such as un côté (m., side) keeps its own gender. Do not treat the written accent in -té as though it were a silent final -e.

With -eur, meaning helps: many nouns naming a quality, such as la largeur (f., width), are feminine. This is not a rule for all words ending in those letters: un moteur (m., engine) names a thing, and even an abstract noun such as le bonheur (m., happiness) can be masculine. Record a new noun with un/une where possible; l' by itself hides gender.
points: When a dictionary contradicts your ending-based guess, keep the dictionary's noun-and-gender pair rather than changing the article to fit the guess.

examples.french: **Le tourisme** crée des emplois.
examples.english: Tourism creates jobs.
examples.note: Le tourisme (m., tourism) illustrates the useful -isme clue.

examples.french: **La sécurité** est importante dans cet atelier.
examples.english: Safety is important in this workshop.
examples.note: La sécurité (f., safety) illustrates -té; un atelier (m.) is a workshop.

examples.french: **L'amitié** compte beaucoup pour nous.
examples.english: Friendship matters a lot to us.
examples.note: Une amitié (f., a friendship) illustrates -tié; the elided definite article alone does not show its gender.

examples.french: **La largeur** de cette porte est suffisante.
examples.english: The width of this door is sufficient.
examples.note: The quality noun largeur is feminine.

examples.french: **Le moteur** est silencieux, et **un côté** du bateau est ouvert.
examples.english: The engine is quiet, and one side of the boat is open.
examples.note: These nouns cannot be assigned feminine gender merely from -eur or -té.

sections.title: An article pattern does not decide the whole sentence
paragraphs: For an obvious body part, keep the ordinary verb that expresses the action. Lever la main means raise your hand; se lever means get up. Adding a reflexive pronoun is not a universal way of translating English your.

Parler français is a common language pattern; parler le français is also possible. This optional article does not make all language nouns optional elsewhere: le français as a sentence subject still needs its article. Likewise, mentioning le docteur differs from directly addressing Docteur. Check the construction, not only the vocabulary.
points: Use these contrasts to avoid overcorrecting a valid sentence just because another sentence uses a different article pattern.

examples.french: Pour répondre, la participante **lève la main**. Ensuite, elle **se lève**.
examples.english: To answer, the participant raises her hand. Then she gets up.
examples.note: The body-part article stays definite; the two verb constructions have different meanings.

examples.french: Il parle **français**. Il parle aussi **le français** avec ses collègues.
examples.english: He speaks French. He also speaks French with his colleagues.
examples.note: Both language constructions are grammatical; the articleless form is very common.

examples.french: **Le docteur** arrive. Bonjour, **docteur** !
examples.english: The doctor is arriving. Hello, doctor!
examples.note: Mentioning the professional and addressing them are different uses.

practice.prompt: Use the -té/-tié clues: supply le or la for '___ sécurité', then un or une for '___ amitié'. Separate the two articles with a comma.
practice.explanation: La sécurité and une amitié are feminine. Using une makes the gender visible where l'amitié would hide it.

practice.prompt: Choose du or des for an unspecified amount of chicken meat: 'La cantine prépare ___ poulet.'
practice.explanation: Here poulet is food in an unspecified amount, not several counted birds.

practice.prompt: Can 'J'aime cette bibliothèque' correctly express liking one particular library?
practice.explanation: Aimer can refer to a particular thing with cette; a preference does not always describe a whole category.

practice.prompt: Supply la or de in each gap, in order separated by a comma: 'Je n'aime pas ___ viande, et je n'achète pas ___ viande.' Both clauses concern meat generally, with no contrastive emphasis.
practice.explanation: The dislike keeps definite la; the second clause denies buying any quantity and uses de.

practice.prompt: Use the -isme gender clue to supply le or la: '___ tourisme'.
practice.explanation: Tourisme is masculine, consistent with the -isme pattern.

practice.prompt: Supply the definite article for the quality noun largeur: '___ largeur du couloir'.
practice.explanation: La largeur is a feminine quality noun in -eur; this does not extend to every -eur noun.

practice.prompt: Use the learned gender, not a mechanical -té rule: '___ côté de la boîte est bleu.' Supply un or une.
practice.explanation: Un côté is masculine despite -té.

practice.prompt: A seated student raises a hand but does not stand up. Choose the intended description.
practice.explanation: The hand-raising action uses lever la main. Se lever would say that she gets up.

practice.prompt: Are both 'Nous parlons français' and 'Nous parlons le français' grammatical language constructions?
practice.explanation: Parler permits the language with or without the article; do not generalise this to all uses of the language noun.

practice.prompt: Remove only the article to turn this into ordinary direct address: 'Merci, le docteur !'
practice.explanation: Directly addressing a doctor does not normally retain the third-person article.

practice.prompt: Supply un or une: '___ décision'.
practice.explanation: Décision is feminine; -sion is a useful clue.

practice.prompt: Use a partitive article: 'Je mange ___ soupe.' (soupe is feminine).
practice.explanation: An unspecified amount of feminine soupe takes de la.

practice.prompt: Combine à + les into one word.
practice.explanation: The contraction is compulsory with the article les.

practice.prompt: For a general preference, complete 'J'aime ___ pain.'
practice.explanation: A general category takes the definite article.

practice.prompt: Supply the partitive for an unspecified amount: 'Il boit ___ lait.' (lait is masculine).
practice.explanation: Du introduces an unspecified amount of masculine lait.

practice.prompt: Use a partitive article: 'Nous avons ___ huile.' (huile is feminine with silent h).
practice.explanation: The silent h allows elision.

practice.prompt: Supply de + le: 'C'est la clé ___ bureau.'
practice.explanation: De + le bureau becomes du bureau.

practice.prompt: Supply à plus the definite article: 'Je vais ___ école.' (école is feminine).
practice.explanation: Before école use l'; à l' does not contract.

practice.prompt: Choose the indefinite article for one item: '___ image'.
practice.explanation: Image is a feminine exception to the common -age pattern.

practice.prompt: Supply the usual definite article: 'Elle se brosse ___ dents.'
practice.explanation: The reflexive construction identifies whose teeth; dents is plural.

practice.prompt: Supply the definite article: '___ mathématiques sont utiles.'
practice.explanation: An academic subject used as a noun takes the article.

practice.prompt: You are talking about, not addressing, Professor Laurent. Choose the normal wording.
practice.explanation: Use the article when referring to someone by this title.

practice.prompt: Use the article for an unspecified plural quantity: 'Je prends ___ épinards.'
practice.explanation: Épinards is plural; an unspecified quantity takes des.

practice.prompt: Combine de + les in 'les noms ___ élèves'.
practice.explanation: De + les becomes des.

practice.prompt: Supply le or les in this familiar clothing description: 'Il a les mains dans ___ poches.'
practice.explanation: Poches is plural. The definite article is natural here because the person whose hands and pockets are meant is clear.

practice.prompt: Does every noun ending in -e have feminine gender?
practice.explanation: Un problème is masculine; learn each noun with its article.

practice.prompt: Use the appropriate article for a general preference: 'J'aime ___ musique classique.' Musique is feminine.
practice.explanation: A general category after aimer takes a definite article, here feminine la.

production_task.prompt: Describe a simple lunch: say what you have in unspecified quantities, then name one food you like in general. Use three different article forms.
production_task.model_answer: J'ai du pain, de la soupe et de l'eau. J'aime les légumes.
production_task.translation: I have some bread, soup and water. I like vegetables.
rubric: Use a definite article for a general preference.
Match gender and number and elide before a vowel.
